input: "They make poor decisions. Better lines mostly help them defend the mistakes." I smile at Caelindra. "I'll bring something short tomorrow. No promises about sentiment." I turn to Ysolde. "I'd like to see your disobedient instrument tonight." Then to Rashid and Ashara: "And tomorrow afternoon, come to the common room if you like. No audience or assessment. Bring your sister's letter if it needs finishing. We could find out whether an hour has to be useful."
output:
The word *useful* seems to catch Rashid more cleanly than the rest. His thumb rests against the stem of his glass; for once, he does not answer at once.

“Fifth bell,” he says at last. “I have weapons work before then. I can spare an hour afterward.” His gaze meets yours, steady but not unfriendly. “The letter remains mine, though. I may bring it. I may not.”

Ashara tears a piece of bread with her teeth. “I have a ranked challenge after noon. If it finishes before fifth bell, I may come.”

“An admirably warm acceptance,” Rashid says.

“You invited me. You did not issue orders.” Her gold eyes shift to you. “And if I lose, I will not be pleasant company.”

Thessaly considers the dark-painted Garveys watching from the walls. “No audience is not a condition this house can fully provide.”

“There are only portraits,” Caelindra says.

“Those are still people who were placed in a room to watch us.”

Caelindra gives this the consideration it perhaps does not deserve, then turns back to you. “Tomorrow after supper. Upper library, south window. Five pages.”

Her violet eyes narrow slightly.

“Not ‘five pages and a further explanatory page.’ Not six pages in small handwriting. If it is sentimental, at least make it technically competent.”

Ysolde’s mouth nearly becomes a smile. “The instrument does not require a story. Finish eating.”

The meal loosens around that. Rashid and Ashara resume their old argument about whether rankings measure skill or merely advertise it; Seraphel laughs into her wine when Ashara calls the distinction “the hobby of people who enjoy losing politely.” Even Aldric’s composure gives way enough for him to hide a smile behind his cup.

Dessert arrives: tart green fruit, honey cream, and dark little biscuits dusted with salt. By the time the servers begin clearing plates, Aldric has excused himself for evening observance, and Seraphel has slipped a sugared plum into her sleeve with the solemnity of a crime.

Ysolde rises and takes a dark weather-cloak from the vestibule peg.

“There are spare cloaks,” she says. “The west terrace will attempt to remove your ears.”
